The platform supports continuous operation through optional cloud-hosted sandbox VMs, allowing clones to work 24/7 even when laptops are closed. It targets various roles beyond engineering, including designers, product managers, and sales teams, providing customizable automation while maintaining user control and security through open-source software and end-to-end encryption.

items.title: Hollywood creatives train AI to replicate screenwriting and production skills amid industry job slump [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Digging the grave of my skills: Hollywood creatives training AI to do their jobs
items.summary:
Award-winning writers, directors, and producers in Hollywood are taking gig work to train AI models in tasks like screenwriting and production scheduling as a way to supplement income during a downturn in entertainment industry jobs. These creatives are paid between $12 and $200 an hour by agencies contracted with major AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI to teach AI systems the intricacies of their professions.

The decline in traditional film and television work, exacerbated by factors like the pandemic, writers' strikes, and reduced streaming investments, has led to a 28% drop in US motion picture and sound recording jobs since 2022. While some industry figures express fatalism about AI's growing role, others see the training work as a necessary adaptation to changing economic realities. AI is increasingly used in production, with companies like Netflix employing it in hundreds of titles, and directors beginning to incorporate the technology into their workflows.

items.originalTitle: I'm becoming AI-blind
items.summary:
A writer reports struggling to focus on work documents that appear to be generated or heavily influenced by AI, describing a phenomenon they call "AI-blindness." This results in repeated misunderstandings and questions about content already provided, as the brain seems to filter out AI-generated text due to its distinctive style and phrasing.

The writer analyzes examples such as design documents with AI-specific language, verbose technical requirements, and marketing decks mixing reasonable strategy with nonsensical technical jargon. They suggest that exposure to low-effort AI-generated content has trained their brain to quickly identify and ignore such text, similar to "banner blindness." This unintended consequence of AI usage is slowing productivity rather than enhancing it, highlighting challenges in integrating AI-generated content into professional communication.

items.originalTitle: Claudette: Make Claude stop talking like a BuzzFeed article
items.summary:
A GitHub project called NoBuzz addresses Claude AI's tendency to generate responses in a verbose, clickbait-like style by using a Gemini CLI tool to translate its output into clearer, more straightforward language. The tool, nicknamed Claudette, processes Claude's replies through Gemini to produce simplified explanations without the original's elaborate phrasing.

NoBuzz was created because Claude often explains technical issues with excessive detail and dramatic flair, which can hinder understanding. The project uses a skill that pipes Claude's responses through Gemini with instructions to rewrite them in plain English, ensuring the output is more concise and easier to comprehend. This approach accepts that prompting alone cannot fully change Claude's style and instead relies on a separate model to rephrase the content verbatim.

items.title: Survey finds 80% of developers view AI coding tools as more addictive than helpful, with many experiencing burnout and workaholism [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: 80% of developers find AI coding more addictive than helpful
items.summary:
A survey of 305 developers reveals that 80% feel their use of AI coding tools has become more of a dependence than an advantage, leading to increased work hours and difficulty disconnecting from work. Many developers report that AI tools, while useful for generating code and troubleshooting, contribute to workaholism and burnout due to their addictive nature and the constant feedback loop they create.

Developers also express frustration with AI-generated code that is often "almost right" but requires significant debugging, leading to what is described as "verification debt." Despite 80% of developers incorporating AI tools into their workflows, trust in AI accuracy has declined, and the pressure to deliver more work using AI assistance may offset time saved on individual tasks, increasing overall workload and operational risks.

items.title: Analysis: AI agents combine unrestricted operational reach with autonomous judgment, merging two previously separate risks in system automation [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: AI agents merged two dangers once kept separate: reach and judgment
items.summary:
A recent analysis explores how AI agents have evolved to merge two distinct risks that were once kept separate: the ability to operate broadly without discretion and the capacity to make autonomous judgments. Traditionally, rule-following processes executed predefined instructions without judgment, while specialized models made limited decisions within narrow scopes. The new generation of AI agents combines these traits, operating with wide reach and independent decision-making, raising novel safety and accountability challenges.

The article contrasts earlier system components—rule-followers that execute commands exactly and guessers that make probabilistic judgments within confined tasks—with emerging AI agents that possess both extensive operational reach and autonomous judgment capabilities. This convergence creates a threshold where the risks of unintended consequences and errors can no longer be contained by previous design boundaries, signaling a shift in how machine identity and accountability must be managed in complex systems.

items.originalSummary:
Eric Topol is a prominent cardiologist known for his research into deploying AI and other technologies to improve healthcare. He considers himself a Demis Hassabis superfan, and when I spoke to him, he enthusiastically recounted scoring a blurb from the Google DeepMind chair for “Super Agers,” Topol’s bestselling 2025 book on longevity. “He’s a hero of mine,” said Topol.

But last week, Topol publicly called out Hassabis—along with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. On X, he criticized Hassabis’ claim in a “60 Minutes” interview that AI will be capable of curing all diseases within the next decade and took Amodei to task for a similar remark.

“Diabetes, Alzheimer’s, heart disease—we don’t have cures for any of those common diseases. To think that in the next five or 10 years new drugs are going to change everything, there’s no precedent for that,” Topol told me. “It’s unrealistic and it sets the expectations for AI too high. It’s hype.”

Topol is not alone in his pushback. Over the past year, I have been taken aback by the steadily mounting drumbeat of social media posts, podcast interviews and blogs where scientists offer staunch criticism of what AI leaders say, which they regard as dangerous hubris. It’s a favorite topic during gossipy side conversations that take place at academic conferences. And in one widely shared blog post, Stanford computer scientist Daphne Koller likened the narrative around AI’s use in science to a belief that magic wands actually exist.

items.originalTitle: Show HN: VinvAI runs and observes your services to find bugs and perf issues
items.summary:
VinvAI has released an open-source tool that runs and monitors Python services and APIs to detect bugs and performance issues, then verifies fixes automatically without requiring code changes. The tool connects runtime traces to source code, uses Thompson sampling to optimize context for coding agents, and only accepts fixes that pass pre-existing acceptance tests.

The system integrates with IDEs and CLI tools, supports semantic search, fault localization, and runtime evidence, and works with popular coding agents like Claude Code and Cursor. VinvAI demonstrated its effectiveness by finding multiple bugs and performance bottlenecks in popular open-source projects, proving fixes with runtime evidence before merging changes upstream.

This approach addresses developer distrust in AI coding tools by automating the verification step, ensuring that only proven fixes are accepted, and reducing dead code and duplication. VinvAI plans to extend support to TypeScript and Go in the future and operates fully locally without telemetry or accounts.

items.summary:
Knowl introduces a persistent memory system for Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex that automatically retires outdated facts instead of appending them, preventing conflicting information accumulation. This approach improves retrieval accuracy from 73% to 90% in end-to-end benchmarks without requiring an API key.

The system integrates with multiple agents via MCP or CLI, supports Node.js environments, and includes a local embedding model for enhanced search. Knowl's memory management marks superseded facts to exclude them from normal retrieval while keeping them accessible through a timeline feature, addressing common issues in append-only memory systems.

Benchmark tests using MemoryAgentBench's corpus and GPT-4o-mini as a reader confirmed Knowl's superior performance compared to other commercial memory systems, with independent reproductions validating the results. The project is open-source and available on GitHub for easy installation and integration.

On Friday, the company announced it had acquired a minority stake in Cloverleaf Infrastructure, its third equity investment in rapid succession in firms that secure real estate and electricity access for data centers in the U.S.

By backing the two-year-old Cloverleaf Infrastructure alongside recent stakes in Lancium and SB Energy, Nvidia is locking in near-term power rights for facilities that could use multiple generations of its chips over many years. That positioning can also help Nvidia head off what some data center developers fear is a looming chip overhang in which energy grid delays and local political pushback leave new AI hardware sitting idle without electricity.

items.title: The New Robotics ‘Arms Race’: Who Can Do the Craziest Hype Video? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The New Robotics ‘Arms Race’: Who Can Do the Craziest Hype Video?
items.summary:
A couple months ago, a humanoid robot was dispatched to the top of Ecuador’s Mount Chimborazo, the surface point farthest from the center of the planet. It was a stunt arranged by Geologic Dome, a nonprofit that uses AI and robotics for nature conservation, which had obtained the robot from the robotics arm of Virtuals Protocol, a crypto startup.

Along with the robot, Geologic Dome sent a videographer, who hauled up three cameras to shoot clips the nonprofit could use to promote its cause. One clip shows the robot, clad in a purple winter coat and black mittens, plodding over the snowy peak. In other footage, it dances its heart out to a swing tune.

Though these clips might give the impression that robots can now rival humans when it comes to mountaineering, the robot had significant help in scaling Mount Chimborazo. A squad of flesh-and-blood people took turns carrying the 70-pound machine for much of the four-day trek to the summit. “We were 10 people, and I think six finished the expedition with back problems,” said Geologic Dome founder Pablo Berlanga Boemare, laughing.

items.summary:
After I released version 1.0, I figured I would have to do the rotations myself. So I sat down with ChatGPT and I didn’t get it to write the code, but I got it to educate me. With a patient, interactive tutor, I was able to finally do what I hadn’t by reading books and asking mathematician friends – I learnt how to use quaternions just enough to make the app work.

So learning doesn’t stop just because I outsource a bunch of thinking to AI. It pushes me to learn more. I like that as an outcome.

— Matt Webb, Galactic Compass 2: now with new augmented reality mode

items.summary:
Barclays has been losing tech bankers lately. 

Last night I reported that Tim Luke, a veteran semiconductor analyst and banker, is leaving the British investment bank to join Morgan Stanley. His position as a vice chairman in technology investment banking will further strengthen Morgan Stanley’s strong semiconductor banking franchise. 

Not too long ago, semiconductor dealmaking was overlooked by Wall Street, as software and internet matchmaking dominated headlines. But that’s changed thanks to the importance of chips in training and running AI. An increase in semiconductor M&A plus the initial public offerings of companies like Cerebras have put a premium on rainmakers with long-standing networks and knowledge in the industry.
